questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Developmental and Health: Animism
questions.learningObjective: Identify animism in a child's description of an object
questions.stem: In an engineer's design brief, a five-year-old calls a stalled elevator 'angry' and refuses to ride it; which Piagetian concept is shown?

options.text: The child attributes intention to a non-living machine, which is animism.
The child is overgeneralising a rule from one elevator to all elevators.
The child lacks the vocabulary to describe mechanical failure accurately.
options.misconception: treats a language gap as the cause of animism

options.text: The child is projecting its own fear onto the elevator's control panel.

questions.explanation: Attributing life or intention to an inanimate object is animism, common in the preoperational stage. The other options describe different processes that do not fit the child's wording.
questions.hint: Look for life attributed to a thing.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Developmental and Health: Assimilation and Accommodation
questions.learningObjective: Identify accommodation when a schema changes

stimulus.body: An engineer's brief describes a toddler who calls every four-wheeled vehicle a car, then after seeing a tractor calls tractors a new kind of vehicle.

questions.stem: Which process is shown when the toddler creates a new vehicle category?

options.text: Assimilation, because the toddler keeps calling vehicles cars.
options.misconception: confuses keeping a label with changing a schema

options.text: Accommodation, because the schema is revised to fit new information.
Equilibration, because balance is restored after confusion.
options.misconception: names a broader process not shown here

options.text: Object permanence, because the tractor still exists when hidden.

questions.explanation: Creating a new category revises the existing schema, which is accommodation. Assimilation would keep the old label unchanged.

questions.stem: A brief gives 2 concrete tasks a child can do and 1 abstract task the child cannot; how many tasks exceed concrete reasoning?

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Developmental and Health: Working a Problem Instead of Recalling It

stimulus.body: An engineer's brief records a pupil who has never seen a pulley problem before yet derives the mechanical advantage from the given diagram.

questions.stem: The pupil's success best shows?

options.text: Animism, because pulleys seem alive.
Recall, because pulley facts are common.
Reasoning, because a novel problem is worked through.
Accommodation, because schemas change.

questions.explanation: A never-seen problem cannot be solved by recall. The pupil must work through the given information.

questions.stem: A child's organised expectation that switches turn things on is a?

options.text: Animism, life attribution.
Scaffolding, temporary support.
Accommodation, schema revision.
Schema, an organised mental framework.

questions.explanation: An organised expectation is a schema. Scaffolding and accommodation name different processes.

questions.subject: PSYCHOLOGY
questions.topic: Developmental and Health: Assimilation and Accommodation
questions.stem: A child revises the 'bird' schema after seeing a penguin that swims; this revision is?

options.text: Assimilation, because the penguin is filed under bird.
Accommodation, because the schema changes to include swimming.
Equilibration, because balance is restored.
Animism, because birds seem alive.

questions.explanation: Revising the schema to include swimming is accommodation. Assimilation would keep the old definition unchanged.

questions.topic: Developmental and Health: Support That Is Withdrawn
questions.stem: A mentor removes hints only after a child completes tasks correctly alone; explain the principle.

answer.exemplar: Support is faded when independent success shows the learner no longer needs it, keeping the task within reach without creating dependency.

questions.explanation: Fading follows demonstrated competence. Removing support too early risks failure; too late risks dependence.

questions.topic: Developmental and Health: Reasoning Well About One Thing and Poorly About Another

stimulus.body: An engineer's brief finds a child conserves number in the morning session but fails mass conservation in the afternoon session of the same day.

questions.stem: This pattern best illustrates?

options.text: Animism, because mass seems alive.
Stage regression, losing a prior ability.
Horizontal decalage, uneven mastery within a stage.
Assimilation, because schemas merge.

questions.explanation: Uneven mastery across related tasks within one day reflects horizontal decalage, not regression or schema merging.

questions.topic: Developmental and Health: Reasoning About Possibilities in Adolescence
questions.stem: An adolescent considers three possible bridge designs before building any; this shows?

options.text: Recall, because designs are memorised.
Concrete reasoning, which needs a model.
Animism, because designs seem alive.
Formal operational reasoning about possibilities.

questions.explanation: Considering multiple possibilities before action is formal operational thought. Concrete reasoning would need a tangible model first.
